title: Is San Diego oversaturated? Short-term vs long-term rental, by the numbers
excerpt: San Diego caps whole-home short-term rentals by law. What the city's license counts, HUD rent data and visitor figures show, and how to compare a home's short-term and long-term income.

seo.title: Is San Diego Oversaturated? STR vs Long-Term Rental 2026
seo.description: San Diego caps whole-home short-term rentals. City license counts, HUD rents and tax rules as of Nov 2026, and how to compare STR and long-term income.

heroCaption: Pacific Beach from the air. Whole-home short-term rentals here count against a citywide cap of 1% of housing units.
bodyHtml:
Owners weighing a San Diego home for short-term rental often hear that the market is oversaturated: too many listings chasing too few guests. The city's own licensing data does not support that description in its simplest form, because whole-home short-term rentals are capped by law. The more useful question is whether a particular home earns more, after costs and effort, as a short-term rental or as a long-term rental. This guide sets out the public numbers for both as of November 2026 and a method for comparing them.

As of November 2026

License counts and fees come from the City Treasurer's STRO page (counts as of November 6, 2026). Tax rates come from the Treasurer's TOT page. Long-term rent figures come from HUD's fiscal year 2026 Fair Market Rents and HUD's San Diego market report (February 2026). Visitor figures come from the San Diego Tourism Authority's 2025 fast facts. Counts and rates change, so check each source before acting.

Is San Diego oversaturated with short-term rentals?

Not in the sense of unlimited supply. The City of San Diego caps whole-home short-term rental licenses at 1% of its housing units outside Mission Beach, and at 30% of housing units inside the Mission Beach planning area. As of November 6, 2026, 4,863 whole-home licenses were issued outside Mission Beach with 798 still available, and Mission Beach had none left. Competition exists, but it happens inside a fixed ceiling.

In most U.S. markets, anyone can list a home, and the number of listings rises until returns fall. San Diego's Short-Term Residential Occupancy (STRO) ordinance works differently. A stay of less than one month is short-term residential occupancy under section 510.0102 of the municipal code, and renting a whole home for more than 20 days a year requires a capped license. Section 510.0104 also says a host "may only hold one license at a time," which limits how many homes a single operator can license in their own name.

What the license counts show

  • Tier 3 (whole home, outside Mission Beach): 4,863 issued and 798 remaining, which puts the cap at about 5,661 licenses.
  • Tier 4 (whole home, Mission Beach): 1,099 issued, none remaining.
  • Tier 2 (home sharing in the host's own residence): 2,331 issued, no cap.
  • Tier 1 (20 days a year or fewer): 135 issued, no cap.

Two readings follow from these numbers. Citywide, the whole-home cap had not been reached as of early November, so licenses were still available outside Mission Beach. In Mission Beach, the cap has been reached, so the number of whole-home rentals there cannot grow until licenses come back into the pool. Our STRO license tracker follows the Tier 3 count from the city's open data.

What the demand side shows

The San Diego Tourism Authority reports 32.4 million visitors to San Diego County in 2025, 17.8 million of them overnight visitors, with $14.4 billion in direct visitor spending. Hotels averaged 72.2% occupancy at an average daily rate of $213. Those are county figures and include hotels, so they do not describe vacation rentals directly. They do show that overnight demand is large relative to a whole-home rental supply capped in the low thousands within the city.

What does a long-term rental earn in San Diego?

HUD's fiscal year 2026 Fair Market Rents for the San Diego metro area are $3,001 a month for a two-bedroom, $3,998 for a three-bedroom and $4,845 for a four-bedroom. HUD's February 2026 market report put the average apartment rent at $2,401 in late 2025, roughly unchanged from a year earlier, with apartment vacancy up to 5.4% from 4.7%.

Fair Market Rents are HUD's estimate of typical gross rent, including utilities, for a standard-quality unit. They are not top-of-market figures, and a renovated coastal house will usually lease above them. They are useful as a public baseline. At the three-bedroom figure, twelve months of rent comes to $47,976 a year before vacancy, repairs, insurance and any leasing fees.

The market report also points to softer conditions for landlords than in recent years. It notes that about 66% of the 7,975 apartment units delivered in the metro area in 2025 were absorbed, and that about 11,400 rental units were under construction. More new supply tends to slow rent growth for existing homes.

What rules apply to each option?

Both paths are regulated, in different ways. Short-term rentals face licensing, a cap and a room tax collected from guests. Long-term rentals face state rent-increase limits and city tenant protections that start on the first day of a tenancy.

Short-term rental (stays under one month)

  • License: a Tier 3 or Tier 4 license costs a $41 application fee plus a $1,129 license fee, both non-refundable, and lasts two years before renewal. Licenses do not transfer when a home sells; see our guide to buying or selling a home with an STRO license.
  • Transient occupancy tax: since May 1, 2025, the city's TOT is 11.75%, 12.75% or 13.75% depending on the home's tax zone. The guest pays it; the operator collects and remits it. The separate 2% Tourism Marketing District assessment applies to lodging businesses with 70 or more rooms.
  • Operating work: cleaning between every stay, guest messaging, restocking, pricing and repairs, done by the owner or a manager.

Long-term rental

  • Rent increases: California's statewide cap, explained by the Attorney General, limits annual increases to 5% plus the change in the cost of living, up to 10%. For San Diego, the maximum is 8.8% for increases taking effect between August 1, 2025 and July 31, 2026, and 8.2% from August 1, 2026 to July 31, 2027. Units newer than 15 years are outside the cap, and single-family homes and condos are covered when a corporation owns them.
  • Tenant protections: the city's Residential Tenant Protections Ordinance, in effect since June 2023, applies from the first day of a tenancy, with an exemption for fixed-term leases of three months or less. A tenant who must leave through no fault of their own is entitled to two months' rent in relocation assistance, or three months for seniors and people with disabilities.
  • Operating work: tenant screening, rent collection and repairs, with far fewer turnovers.

A third option sits between them. Furnished stays of one month or longer fall outside STRO licensing and TOT under the code's definitions. They earn less per night than short stays and more per month than an unfurnished lease in many coastal areas, with fewer turnovers than either.

How should an owner compare short-term and long-term income?

Compare net income, not gross. Start with the long-term rent a home could realistically command, subtract vacancy and the owner's costs, and treat that net figure as the bar. Then estimate what the home would need to clear per booked night, after cleaning, utilities, supplies, furnishings and management, to beat it. If the required net nightly figure is well within what comparable licensed homes achieve, short-term rental is worth a closer look.

A worked example using the HUD three-bedroom figure shows how the bar moves with occupancy. To match $47,976 a year, a short-term rental would need to net:

  • about $320 per booked night at 150 nights a year;
  • about $240 per booked night at 200 nights a year;
  • about $192 per booked night at 250 nights a year.

"Net" here means after the costs a long-term landlord usually does not carry: cleaning, utilities, internet, consumables, platform fees, furnishing and its replacement, and management. The guest's TOT is not part of the owner's revenue and should be left out of both sides. The example uses HUD's baseline rent, so an owner of a home that would lease well above it should substitute a real lease comparable.

The comparison also has inputs that are not dollars:

  • Who does the work. A short-term rental needs attention every week; a long-term rental needs attention at move-in, move-out and repairs.
  • Personal use. A short-term rental calendar can hold weeks for the owner. A leased home is unavailable for the lease term.
  • Licensing risk. A Tier 3 license must be obtained, renewed every two years and kept in good standing, and it ends if the home is sold.
  • Exit flexibility. Ending a long-term tenancy is governed by just-cause rules and relocation payments. A short-term calendar can be closed after the last booked stay.

When does a long-term rental make more sense?

A long-term lease tends to fit when the home cannot get a whole-home license, when it sits far from the beaches, downtown and other visitor draws, or when the owner wants predictable monthly income with little involvement. In Mission Beach today, a home without an existing Tier 4 license cannot be rented whole for short stays more than 20 days a year.

It also fits homes whose likely nightly rate would not clear the bar in the example above once operating costs are counted. A modest inland home near a large employer may lease quickly at a strong rent and draw few vacation guests.

When does a short-term rental make more sense?

Short-term rental tends to fit homes near the coast or other visitor demand, with a license available, with the space and finish guests pay for, and with an owner who either wants to run it or will hire someone who does. Homes that photograph well and sleep groups usually command higher nightly rates; our post on design choices that lift the nightly rate covers the specifics.

Neighborhood matters as much as the home. Our comparison of La Jolla and Pacific Beach shows two markets a few miles apart with different guests, booking windows and turnover patterns. Our guide to what a San Diego home could earn explains how rate, seasonality and design combine into an annual figure.

So is it too late to start a short-term rental in San Diego?

Outside Mission Beach, no: licenses remained available as of November 6, 2026. What has changed is where the competition happens. With supply capped, homes compete on rate, reviews, photos and pricing discipline rather than on being one of few listings. A well-run home in a strong location can still clear the long-term bar comfortably; a home with an average setup and static pricing may not.

Cardo reports that the homes it manages outperform their market by up to 32%. For a specific home, a comparison of its likely short-term revenue against a realistic long-term lease is the clearest way to decide. Owners can request a free earning estimate, and our management fees page lists what the service includes and what it costs.

This article is general information about San Diego rules and public market data as of November 2026. It is not tax, legal or financial advice. Confirm current rules with the City of San Diego and talk to a qualified professional about your situation.
